text: Basanti Dulal Nag Chaudhuri (6 September 1917 – 25 June 2006) was an Indian nuclear scientist and academic who served as Scientific Advisor to the Ministry of Defence, Government of India, and played a pivotal role in India's nuclear program. He is recognized as one of the pioneers of nuclear physics in India. As Director General of the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), he was instrumental in Pokhran-I (Smiling Buddha), India's first successful nuclear bomb test on 18 May 1974, which made India the sixth nation in the world to become a nuclear superpower, following the United States of America, Soviet Union (now Russia), England, France, and China. He also initiated the first feasibility studies on India's ballistic missile program. Born into a Bengali Hindu family in Narayanganj, Dhaka, Bengal Presidency, British India (present-day Bangladesh), his family relocated to West Bengal, India, following the partition of India in 1947 and the communal violence in East Bengal. His father became a professor of English at Banaras Hindu University (now IIT-BHU), Varanasi. Nagchaudhuri earned a Bachelor of Science degree from Banaras Hindu University and a Master's degree from Allahabad University. In Allahabad, he met lawyer Parmeshwar Narayan Haksar and renowned physicist Meghnad Saha, with whom he became close and joined his research group. In July 1938, when Saha moved to Rajabazar Science College, University of Calcutta, Nagchaudhuri followed. With Saha's support and funding from the Tatas, he moved to the University of California, Berkeley in 1938 to pursue a doctorate in Nuclear Physics, under Ernest Lawrence, completing it in 1941. After returning to India, he joined Saha's research group at Rajabazar Science College and, in 1949, became affiliated with the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics (SINP), later serving as its Director after Saha's retirement in 1952. His research focused on nuclear isomers, induced radioactivity, Cherenkov radiation, and nonthermal plasma. Before returning to India, he had arranged for the shipment of parts for a cyclotron magnet to Calcutta University, but the second consignment was sunk by the Japanese; the team, led by Saha and later Nagchaudhuri, built the remaining components, overcoming persistent issues with vacuum pumps and demountable oscillators. The cyclotron began functioning in 1954 after Emilio Segre's visit, and Nagchaudhuri is credited with building the first cyclotron in India. In 1953, he succeeded Meghnad Saha as Palit Professor of Physics at Calcutta University, holding the position until 1959. He was a visiting professor at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1961–62 and was nominated as a Lincoln Lecturer. Through his connections with B.C. Roy and P.N. Haksar, he was appointed Chairman of the Cabinet Committee on Science & Technology from 1969 to 1972 and served as Scientific Advisor to the Ministry of Defence during this period. He became a Member of the Planning Commission in 1970 and served as Scientific Advisor to the DRDO from 1970 to 1974. In October 1972, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi approved the Smiling Buddha test, and Nagchaudhuri was a member of the steering committee for its preparations. The explosive lenses for the test were fabricated in the DRDO laboratories under his leadership. In 1970, he was tasked by Indira Gandhi to prepare a classified feasibility study for long-range ballistic missiles, leading to the initiation of Project Valiant in 1972 to develop a liquid-fuelled intermediate-range ballistic missile and Project Devil at DRDL for short-range surface-to-air missiles. Both projects were terminated in 1974 due to internal conflicts and lack of progress but laid the groundwork for the Integrated Guided Missile Development Program in the early 1980s. In 1970–71, he chaired a committee on India's maritime security, recommending coastal patrols, a registry of offshore fishing vessels, and a force to intercept illegal vessels—recommendations that formed the basis of the Rustamji Committee in 1974, leading to the establishment of the Indian Coast Guard. From 1 July 1974 to 1 January 1979, he served as Vice Chancellor of Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). From 1975 to 1977, he chaired the National Committee on Environmental Planning and Coordination. He also served on the Board of Governors of the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. Nagchaudhuri was a member of numerous Indian and international scientific councils, including the Scientific Council of the International Centre for Theoretical Physics from 1976 to 1984 and the Research Advisory Council of the National Physical Laboratory from 1980 to 1982, and served as a member and vice-chair of the Board of Governors of the East-West Center. He also served on the boards of Bharat Dynamics Limited, Bharat Electronics Limited, and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited. He maintained an active interest in Hindustani Classical Music and Bengali literature and culture. He was elected a Fellow of the Indian National Science Academy in 1964, awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 1975, and received honorary doctorates from Andhra University and Kanpur University. He died of a cerebral infarction on 25 June 2006 and was survived by his wife, Dipali Nag, his son, and his family.
